'''Daniel E. Lieberman''' (born June 3, 1964) is a [[paleoanthropologist]] at [[Harvard University]], where he is the Edwin M Lerner II Professor of [[Biology|Biological Sciences]], and Professor in the Department of Human Evolutionary Biology. He is best known for his research on [[running]], the [[evolution]] of the [[human head]]<ref name="headbook" /> and the [[human body]],<ref name="storybook" /> and for studying how human evolutionary history, especially in terms of physical activity and diet, can improve human health.<ref name="exercised" /><ref name="fedup" />

== Biography ==
Lieberman grew up in [[Connecticut]] and [[Rhode Island]]. After attending [[Classical High School]] in [[Providence, Rhode Island]], Lieberman attended [[Harvard University]], where he received his B.A. ''[[Latin honors|summa cum laude]]'' in [[biological anthropology]] (1986) and joint M.A. and Ph.D. degrees in biological anthropology and archaeology (1993).<ref name="cv" /> He also received an M.Phil. (1987) from [[University of Cambridge|Cambridge University]],<ref name="cv" /> where he was a [[Frank Knox Memorial Fellowship|Frank Knox Memorial Fellow]]. Following his Ph.D., he was a Junior Fellow in the [[Harvard Society of Fellows]] (1993–1996). He then taught at [[Rutgers University]] (1995–1998) and the [[George Washington University]] (1998–2001) before becoming a professor at Harvard University in 2001.<ref name="cv" />

In 2009, Lieberman became the founding chair of Harvard University's Department of Human Evolutionary Biology.<ref name="gazette2009">{{cite news |last=Bradt |first=Steve |date=May 28, 2009 |title=New department reflects the evolution of human evolution |work=[[Harvard University|Harvard Gazette]] |url=https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2009/05/new-department-reflects-the-evolution-of-human-evolution/ |access-date=July 29, 2026}}</ref> He served as chair from 2009 to 2018, and from 2022 to 2025.<ref name="cv" /> In addition to being director of the Skeletal Biology and Biomechanics Laboratory at Harvard, Lieberman is on the curatorial board of the [[Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology]], a member of the Department of Organismic and Evolutionary Biology at Harvard, and the Scientific Executive Committee of the [[Leakey Foundation|L.S.B. Leakey Foundation]].<ref name="cv" />

== Scientific work ==
Lieberman has mostly studied how and why the human body evolved to be the way it is, especially in regards to physical activity and diet, and how that evolutionary history is relevant for health.

=== Evolution of the human head ===
For the first half of his career, Lieberman's research primarily focused on integrating comparative and fossil anatomy, experimental biomechanics, and developmental biology to explore hominin craniofacial function and evolution. He summarized much of this research in his 2011 book, ''The Evolution of the Human Head''.<ref name="headbook" /> A key contribution was to show that many of the features used to classify ''[[Homo sapiens]]'' result from a more retracted, smaller face which causes a more flexed [[Base of skull|cranial base]] that in turn sets up a more globular [[cranial vault]].<ref name="cranialform2002">{{cite journal |last1=Lieberman |first1=Daniel E. |last2=McBratney |first2=Brandeis M. |last3=Krovitz |first3=Gail |title=The evolution and development of cranial form in ''Homo sapiens'' |journal=[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]] |volume=99 |issue=3 |pages=1134–1139 |year=2002 |doi=10.1073/pnas.022440799 |pmid=11805284 |pmc=122156 |doi-access=free}}</ref> In other papers, Lieberman with colleagues showed how this integrated configuration has implications for a range of functions and adaptations including speech, swallowing, and head balance during locomotion.<ref name="speculations2008">{{cite journal |last=Lieberman |first=Daniel E. |title=Speculations about the selective basis for modern human craniofacial form |journal=[[Evolutionary Anthropology (journal)|Evolutionary Anthropology]] |volume=17 |issue=1 |pages=55–68 |year=2008 |doi=10.1002/evan.20154}}</ref>

Lieberman has also worked on many other aspects of hominin craniofacial evolution. Of particular note, he worked with [[Michel Brunet (paleontologist)|Michel Brunet]] and colleagues to describe and analyze the oldest known hominin species, ''[[Sahelanthropus tchadensis]]'',<ref name="brunet2002">{{cite journal |last1=Brunet |first1=Michel |display-authors=etal |last2=Guy |first2=Franck |last3=Pilbeam |first3=David |title=A new hominid from the Upper Miocene of Chad, Central Africa |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |volume=418 |issue=6894 |pages=145–151 |year=2002 |doi=10.1038/nature00879 |pmid=12110880 |bibcode=2002Natur.418..145B}}</ref><ref name="zollikofer2005">{{cite journal |last1=Zollikofer |first1=Christoph P. E. |display-authors=etal |last2=Ponce de León |first2=Marcia S. |last3=Lieberman |first3=Daniel E. |title=Virtual cranial reconstruction of ''Sahelanthropus tchadensis'' |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |volume=434 |issue=7034 |pages=755–759 |year=2005 |doi=10.1038/nature03397 |pmid=15815628 |bibcode=2005Natur.434..755Z |url=http://doc.rero.ch/record/15309/files/PAL_E2608.pdf}}</ref><ref name="guy2005">{{cite journal |last1=Guy |first1=Franck |display-authors=etal |last2=Lieberman |first2=Daniel E. |last3=Pilbeam |first3=David |title=Morphological affinities of the ''Sahelanthropus tchadensis'' (Late Miocene hominid from Chad) cranium |journal=[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]] |volume=102 |issue=52 |pages=18836–18841 |year=2005 |doi=10.1073/pnas.0509564102 |pmid=16380424 |pmc=1323204 |doi-access=free}}</ref> and with [[David Pilbeam]] to argue that the first hominins likely evolved from a last common ancestor with chimpanzees that largely resembled extant chimpanzees.<ref name="pilbeam2017">{{cite book |last1=Pilbeam |first1=David R. |last2=Lieberman |first2=Daniel E. |chapter=Reconstructing the last common ancestor of chimpanzees and humans |editor1-last=Muller |editor1-first=Martin N. |editor2-last=Wrangham |editor2-first=Richard W. |editor3-last=Pilbeam |editor3-first=David R. |title=Chimpanzees and Human Evolution |publisher=[[Harvard University Press]] |location=Cambridge, Massachusetts |year=2017 |isbn=978-0-674-96795-3}}</ref> Lieberman also published on the challenges of using craniofacial data to reconstruct evolutionary relationships among hominins,<ref name="homoplasy1996">{{cite journal |last1=Lieberman |first1=Daniel E. |last2=Wood |first2=Bernard A. |last3=Pilbeam |first3=David R. |title=Homoplasy and early ''Homo'': an analysis of the evolutionary relationships of ''H. habilis'' sensu stricto and ''H. rudolfensis'' |journal=[[Journal of Human Evolution]] |volume=30 |issue=2 |pages=97–120 |year=1996 |doi=10.1006/jhev.1996.0008}}</ref> and on the evolutionary biomechanics of mastication, including a study with Katherine Zink showing that mechanically processing meat and [[Storage organ|underground storage organs]] with [[Oldowan]] stone tools considerably increases the efficiency and effectiveness of chewing and likely made possible selection for reduced tooth size in the genus ''[[Homo]]''.<ref name="zink2016">{{cite journal |last1=Zink |first1=Katherine D. |last2=Lieberman |first2=Daniel E. |title=Impact of meat and Lower Palaeolithic food processing techniques on chewing in humans |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |volume=531 |issue=7595 |pages=500–503 |year=2016 |doi=10.1038/nature16990 |pmid=26958832 |bibcode=2016Natur.531..500Z}}</ref>

=== Skeletal biomechanics ===
Because mechanical forces affect skeletal morphology and vice versa, much of Lieberman's research has tested how behaviors such as chewing, walking and running load the musculoskeletal system and influence how bones grow. Many of these studies involve experimentally testing biomechanical models of human or hominin anatomical variations in humans and model organisms in the lab. Lieberman and colleagues showed that loading from locomotion causes sheep to grow more bone in proximal limb bones almost entirely when they are immature and to repair bone as adults, especially in distal elements.<ref name="bonegrowth2003">{{cite journal |last1=Lieberman |first1=Daniel E. |last2=Pearson |first2=Osbjorn M. |last3=Polk |first3=John D. |last4=Demes |first4=Brigitte |last5=Crompton |first5=Alfred W. |title=Optimization of bone growth and remodeling in response to loading in tapered mammalian limbs |journal=[[The Journal of Experimental Biology]] |volume=206 |issue=18 |pages=3125–3138 |year=2003 |doi=10.1242/jeb.00514 |pmid=12909694 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Lieberman and colleagues also showed that the cross-sectional geometry of these bones does not accurately reflect the orientations in which they are loaded. These experiments call into question using cross sections of human and other hominin limb bones to infer how they walked and ran.<ref name="crosssection2004">{{cite journal |last1=Lieberman |first1=Daniel E. |last2=Polk |first2=John D. |last3=Demes |first3=Brigitte |title=Predicting long bone loading from cross-sectional geometry |journal=[[American Journal of Biological Anthropology|American Journal of Physical Anthropology]] |volume=123 |issue=2 |pages=156–171 |year=2004 |doi=10.1002/ajpa.10316 |pmid=14730649}}</ref> In other experiments, Lieberman showed that processing food causes the upper and lower jaws to grow less in model organisms ([[hyrax]]es) that, like humans, have retracted faces, thus causing dental crowding and increasing the risk of impacted [[Wisdom tooth|wisdom teeth]].<ref name="hyrax2004">{{cite journal |last1=Lieberman |first1=Daniel E. |last2=Krovitz |first2=Gail E. |last3=Yates |first3=Franklin W. |last4=Devlin |first4=Maureen |last5=St Claire |first5=Marisa |title=Effects of food processing on masticatory strain and craniofacial growth in a retrognathic face |journal=[[Journal of Human Evolution]] |volume=46 |issue=6 |pages=655–677 |year=2004 |doi=10.1016/j.jhevol.2004.03.005 |pmid=15183669}}</ref> Experiments with [[Alfred W. Crompton|A. W. Crompton]] showed that fusion of the [[mandibular symphysis]] in primates and other species like wombats transfers forces from muscles on the non-chewing side of the head to increase bite forces.<ref name="symphysis2000">{{cite journal |last1=Lieberman |first1=Daniel E. |last2=Crompton |first2=Alfred W. |title=Why fuse the mandibular symphysis? A comparative analysis |journal=[[American Journal of Biological Anthropology|American Journal of Physical Anthropology]] |volume=112 |issue=4 |pages=517–540 |year=2000 |doi=10.1002/1096-8644(200008)112:4<517::AID-AJPA7>3.0.CO;2-4 |pmid=10918127}}</ref>

=== Evolution of human physical activity ===

==== Running ====
Lieberman is best known for his work on the evolution of running. Building off a proposal by David Carrier,<ref name="carrier1984">{{cite journal |last=Carrier |first=David R. |title=The energetic paradox of human running and hominid evolution |journal=[[Current Anthropology]] |volume=25 |issue=4 |pages=483–495 |year=1984 |doi=10.1086/203165}}</ref> he and Dennis Bramble developed the [[endurance running hypothesis]], which proposes that between 3 and 2 million years ago, the genus ''Homo'' evolved anatomical and physiological adaptations for long-distance running as part of hunter-gatherer lifestyles. In their 2004 "Born to Run" paper in the journal ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'', entitled "Endurance running and the evolution of ''Homo''", he and Bramble reviewed how effective humans are at distance running, identified a long list of traits that improve endurance running performance, showed that these traits first appear in the genus ''Homo'', especially ''[[Homo erectus]]'', and argued that endurance running likely evolved to permit [[persistence hunting]].<ref name="bramble2004">{{cite journal |last1=Bramble |first1=Dennis M. |last2=Lieberman |first2=Daniel E. |title=Endurance running and the evolution of ''Homo'' |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |volume=432 |issue=7015 |pages=345–352 |year=2004 |doi=10.1038/nature03052 |pmid=15549097 |bibcode=2004Natur.432..345B |url=http://doc.rero.ch/record/15289/files/PAL_E2588.pdf}}</ref> These traits, which Lieberman and his students and others have studied and tested experimentally in a series of papers, include an enlarged [[gluteus maximus]];<ref name="glutmax2006">{{cite journal |last1=Lieberman |first1=Daniel E. |last2=Raichlen |first2=David A. |last3=Pontzer |first3=Herman |last4=Bramble |first4=Dennis M. |last5=Cutright-Smith |first5=Elizabeth |title=The human gluteus maximus and its role in running |journal=[[The Journal of Experimental Biology]] |volume=209 |issue=11 |pages=2143–2155 |year=2006 |doi=10.1242/jeb.02255 |pmid=16709916 |doi-access=free}}</ref> short toes;<ref name="shorttoes2009">{{cite journal |last1=Rolian |first1=Campbell |last2=Lieberman |first2=Daniel E. |last3=Hamill |first3=Joseph |last4=Scott |first4=John W. |last5=Werbel |first5=William |title=Walking, running and the evolution of short toes in humans |journal=[[The Journal of Experimental Biology]] |volume=212 |issue=5 |pages=713–721 |year=2009 |doi=10.1242/jeb.019885 |pmid=19218523 |doi-access=free}}</ref> a [[Arches of the foot|longitudinal arch]] in the foot;<ref name="foot2018">{{cite journal |last1=Holowka |first1=Nicholas B. |last2=Lieberman |first2=Daniel E. |title=Rethinking the evolution of the human foot: insights from experimental research |journal=[[The Journal of Experimental Biology]] |volume=221 |issue=17 |article-number=jeb174425 |year=2018 |doi=10.1242/jeb.174425 |pmid=30190415 |doi-access=free}}</ref> elongated, spring-like tendons in the leg such as the [[Achilles tendon|Achilles]] and [[iliotibial tract|iliotibial band]];<ref name="itb2015">{{cite journal |last1=Eng |first1=Carolyn M. |last2=Arnold |first2=Allison S. |last3=Lieberman |first3=Daniel E. |last4=Biewener |first4=Andrew A. |title=The capacity of the human iliotibial band to store elastic energy during running |journal=Journal of Biomechanics |volume=48 |issue=12 |pages=3341–3348 |year=2015 |doi=10.1016/j.jbiomech.2015.06.017 |pmid=26162548}}</ref> a [[nuchal ligament]] for head stabilization;<ref name="headforearm2021">{{cite journal |last1=Yegian |first1=Andrew K. |last2=Tucker |first2=Yanish |last3=Bramble |first3=Dennis M. |last4=Lieberman |first4=Daniel E. |title=Neuromechanical linkage between the head and forearm during running |journal=[[American Journal of Biological Anthropology|American Journal of Physical Anthropology]] |volume=174 |issue=4 |pages=752–762 |year=2021 |doi=10.1002/ajpa.24234 |pmid=33491216}}</ref> long legs;<ref name="limblength2007">{{cite journal |last=Pontzer |first=Herman |title=Effective limb length and the scaling of locomotor cost in terrestrial animals |journal=[[The Journal of Experimental Biology]] |volume=210 |issue=10 |pages=1752–1761 |year=2007 |doi=10.1242/jeb.002246 |pmid=17488938 |doi-access=free}}</ref> lack of fur and an elaboration of [[sweat gland]]s to permit efficient sweating;<ref name="heatloss2015">{{cite journal |last=Lieberman |first=Daniel E. |title=Human locomotion and heat loss: an evolutionary perspective |journal=[[Comprehensive Physiology]] |volume=5 |issue=1 |pages=99–117 |year=2015 |doi=10.1002/cphy.c140011 |pmid=25589265}}</ref><ref name="sweat2015">{{cite journal |last1=Kamberov |first1=Yana G. |display-authors=etal |last2=Karlsson |first2=Elinor K. |last3=Kamberova |first3=Gerda L. |title=A genetic basis of variation in eccrine sweat gland and hair follicle density |journal=[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]] |volume=112 ventilation;<ref name="thoracic2019">{{cite journal |last1=Callison |first1=W. ==== Barefoot running ====
Lieberman also conducted experiments with Madhusudan Venkadesan and others on barefoot versus shod running, showing that many habitually barefoot runners often adopt forefoot or midfoot strikes that reduce the impact peak caused by the collision of the foot with the ground.<ref name="barefoot2010">{{cite journal |last1=Lieberman |first1=Daniel E. |display-authors=etal |last2=Venkadesan |first2=Madhusudhan |last3=Werbel |first3=William A. |title=Foot strike patterns and collision forces in habitually barefoot versus shod runners |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |volume=463 |issue=7280 |pages=531–535 |year=2010 |doi=10.1038/nature08723 |pmid=20111000 |bibcode=2010Natur.463..531L}}</ref> Lieberman and colleagues have published studies claiming that forefoot or midfoot striking may help prevent some running injuries,<ref name="injury2012">{{cite journal |last1=Daoud |first1=Adam I. |last2=Geissler |first2=Gary J. |last3=Wang |first3=Frank |last4=Saretsky |first4=Jason |last5=Daoud |first5=Yahya A. |last6=Lieberman |first6=Daniel E. |title=Foot strike and injury rates in endurance runners: a retrospective study |journal=[[Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise]] |volume=44 |issue=7 |pages=1325–1334 |year=2012 |doi=10.1249/MSS.0b013e3182465115 |pmid=22217561}}</ref><ref name="essr2012">{{cite journal |last=Lieberman |first=Daniel E. |title=What we can learn about running from barefoot running: an evolutionary medical perspective |journal=[[Exercise and Sport Sciences Reviews]] |volume=40 |issue=2 |pages=63–72 |year=2012 |doi=10.1097/JES.0b013e31824ab210 |pmid=22257937 |doi-access=free}}</ref> and promote stronger feet.<ref name="footstrength2018">{{cite journal |last1=Holowka |first1=Nicholas B. |last2=Wallace |first2=Ian J. |last3=Lieberman |first3=Daniel E. |title=Foot strength and stiffness are related to footwear use in a comparison of minimally- vs. conventionally-shod populations |journal=[[Scientific Reports]] |volume=8 |issue=1 |pages=3679 |year=2018 |doi=10.1038/s41598-018-21916-7  |doi-access=free|pmid=29487321 |pmc=5829167}}</ref> These studies have stimulated considerable research on running biomechanics. Lieberman and colleagues also showed that calluses, which barefoot individuals normally develop, protect the foot from injury without compromising [[Mechanoreceptor|mechanosensation]].<ref name="callus2019">{{cite journal |last1=Holowka |first1=Nicholas B. |display-authors=etal |last2=Wynands |first2=Bert |last3=Drechsel |first3=Tina J. |title=Foot callus thickness does not trade off protection for tactile sensitivity during walking |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |volume=571 |issue=7764 |pages=261–264 |year=2019 |doi=10.1038/s41586-019-1345-6 |pmid=31243365}}</ref> Many of Lieberman's insights on running were popularized in the book ''[[Born to Run (McDougall book)|Born to Run]]'',<ref name="borntorun">{{cite book |last=McDougall |first=Christopher |title=Born to Run: A Hidden Tribe, Superathletes, and the Greatest Race the World Has Never Seen |publisher=[[Alfred A. Knopf|Knopf]] |year=2009 |isbn=978-0-307-26630-9 |url=https://archive.org/details/borntorunhiddent00mcdo/page/304 |url-access=registration |page=[https://archive.org/details/borntorunhiddent00mcdo/page/304 304]}}</ref> but Lieberman has questioned some aspects of the book, including its characterization of [[Rarámuri|Tarahumara]] running and runners as "the myth of the athletic savage".<ref name="tarahumara2020">{{cite journal |last1=Lieberman |first1=Daniel E. |last2=Mahaffey |first2=Mickey |last3=Cubesare Quimare |first3=Silvino |last4=Holowka |first4=Nicholas B. |last5=Wallace |first5=Ian J. |last6=Baggish |first6=Aaron L. |title=Running in Tarahumara (Rarámuri) culture: persistence hunting, footracing, dancing, work, and the fallacy of the athletic savage |journal=[[Current Anthropology]] |volume=61 |issue=3 |pages=356–379 |year=2020 |doi=10.1086/708810|doi-access=free }}</ref> Lieberman is an avid runner, including marathons. He sometimes runs barefoot, and has studied barefoot running, which earned him the nickname "the Barefoot Professor".<ref name="barefootprofessor">{{cite web |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7jrnj-7YKZE |title=Barefoot Professor |publisher=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |access-date=September 25, 2013}}</ref>

==== Walking ====
Lieberman also worked on the evolution of bipedal walking and posture. In collaboration with Michel Brunet and others, he analyzed the cranium of ''Sahelanthropus tchadensis'', the oldest known hominin species, showing that its inferiorly oriented [[foramen magnum]] indicates the species was an upright biped of some sort.<ref name="zollikofer2005" /> With Katherine Whitcome and Liza Shapiro, he showed that hominin females evolved adaptations to cope with the extra load of bearing a fetus during pregnancy.<ref name="fetalload2007">{{cite journal |last1=Whitcome |first1=Katherine K. |last2=Shapiro |first2=Liza J. |last3=Lieberman |first3=Daniel E. |title=Fetal load and the evolution of lumbar lordosis in bipedal hominins |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |volume=450 |issue=7172 |pages=1075–1078 |year=2007 |doi=10.1038/nature06342 |pmid=18075592 |bibcode=2007Natur.450.1075W |url=https://dash.harvard.edu/bitstream/handle/1/3743553/27881641.pdf?sequence=1}}</ref> And in conjunction with Anna Warrener and other colleagues, he showed that female humans walk just as efficiently as males despite having wider pelves, contradicting the [[obstetrical dilemma|obstetric dilemma]] hypothesis.<ref name="pelvis2015">{{cite journal |last1=Warrener |first1=Anna G. |last2=Lewton |first2=Kristi L. |last3=Pontzer |first3=Herman |last4=Lieberman |first4=Daniel E. |title=A wider pelvis does not increase locomotor cost in humans, with implications for the evolution of childbirth |journal=[[PLOS One]] |volume=10 |issue=3 |article-number=e0118903 |year=2015 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0118903 |pmid=25760381 |pmc=4356512 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

==== Throwing ====
Lieberman, Neil Roach, Madhusudan Venkadesan and Michael Rainbow showed that the genus ''Homo'' evolved unique anatomical features enabling high-speed overhand throwing, including elastic energy storage in a wide, horizontally oriented shoulder, as well as other features such as low humeral torsion, a mobile waist, and hyperextensible wrists. They proposed that these adaptations evolved in ''Homo erectus'' for hunting.<ref name="throwing2013">{{cite journal |last1=Roach |first1=Neil T. |last2=Venkadesan |first2=Madhusudhan |last3=Rainbow |first3=Michael J. |last4=Lieberman |first4=Daniel E. |title=Elastic energy storage in the shoulder and the evolution of high-speed throwing in ''Homo'' |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |volume=498 |issue=7455 |pages=483–486 |year=2013 |doi=10.1038/nature12267 |pmid=23803849 |pmc=3785139 |bibcode=2013Natur.498..483R}}</ref>

==== Metabolism ====
Lieberman's research on physical activity also explores how physical activity affects metabolism and health. His active grandparent hypothesis proposes that human hunter-gatherers evolved to be highly physically active throughout their lifespan, including after they stop reproducing, thereby activating repair and maintenance mechanisms that extend healthspan and lifespan.<ref name="grandparent2021">{{cite journal |last1=Lieberman |first1=Daniel E. |last2=Kistner |first2=Timothy M. |last3=Richard |first3=Daniel |last4=Lee |first4=I-Min |last5=Baggish |first5=Aaron L. |title=The active grandparent hypothesis: physical activity and the evolution of extended human healthspans and lifespans |journal=[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]] |volume=118 |issue=50 |article-number=e2107621118 |year=2021 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2107621118 |pmid=34810239 |pmc=8685690 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Using a new method to compare metabolic rates using quotients, Lieberman and colleagues also proposed that humans evolved uniquely high resting, activity, and total metabolic rates by overcoming energy allocation tradeoffs and thermoregulatory constraints that limit other primates, enabling humans to evolve large brains, high reproductive rates, extended longevity, and active lifestyles.<ref name="metabolism2024">{{cite journal |last1=Yegian |first1=Andrew K. |display-authors=etal |last2=Heymsfield |first2=Steven B. |last3=Castillo |first3=Eric R. |title=Metabolic scaling, energy allocation tradeoffs, and the evolution of humans' unique metabolism |journal=[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]] |volume=121 |issue=48 |article-number=e2409674121 |year=2024 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2409674121 |pmid=39556743 |pmc=11621513 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Mismatch and dysevolution ===
Lieberman has advanced the concept of [[evolutionary mismatch]], which he defines as "conditions that are more common or severe because the body is inadequately or imperfectly adapted to novel environmental conditions".<ref name="storybook" /> In his books and many of his papers he synthesizes evidence showing how physical inactivity, energy-dense diets, and other novel environmental factors including highly cushioned shoes contribute to mismatch conditions such as obesity, [[type 2 diabetes]], [[cardiovascular disease]], and flat feet. As an example, in conjunction with Ian Wallace, Lieberman showed that the prevalence of knee [[osteoarthritis]] has more than doubled since the mid-20th century, even after accounting for increased longevity and obesity, indicating that recent environmental and lifestyle changes, especially reduced physical activity, substantially increased disease risk.<ref name="kneeoa2017">{{cite journal |last1=Wallace |first1=Ian J. |display-authors=etal |last2=Worthington |first2=Steven |last3=Felson |first3=David T. |title=Knee osteoarthritis has doubled in prevalence since the mid-20th century |journal=[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]] |volume=114 |issue=35 |pages=9332–9336 |year=2017 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1703856114 |pmid=28808025 |pmc=5584421 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Lieberman divides mismatches into three categories: mismatches of too much (such as sugar), too little (such as physical activity), or too novel (such as tobacco). He further proposes that treating the symptoms not causes of mismatch conditions causes a form of cultural evolution he terms dysevolution, which perpetuates and sometimes worsens the condition.<ref name="storybook" />

=== Diet ===
Lieberman is also interested in using evolutionary perspectives to study human diets. In 2023, he and his colleagues showed that the diets of tropical hunter-gatherers are unlike the [[Paleolithic diet|Paleodiet]] and much more variable.<ref name="diet2023">{{cite journal |last1=Lieberman |first1=Daniel E. |display-authors=etal |last2=Worthington |first2=Steven |last3=Schell |first3=Laura D. |title=Comparing measured dietary variation within and between tropical hunter-gatherer groups to the Paleo Diet |journal=[[The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition]] |volume=118 |issue=3 |pages=549–560 |year=2023 |doi=10.1016/j.ajcnut.2023.06.013 |pmid=37343704 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Lieberman is a co-author on the [[carbohydrate–insulin model]] proposed by [[David Ludwig (physician)|David Ludwig]].<ref name="ludwig2021">{{cite journal |last1=Ludwig |first1=David S. |display-authors=etal |last2=Aronne |first2=Louis J. |last3=Astrup |first3=Arne |title=The carbohydrate-insulin model: a physiological perspective on the obesity pandemic |journal=[[The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition]] |volume=114 |issue=6 |pages=1873–1885 |year=2021 |doi=10.1093/ajcn/nqab270 |pmid=34515299 |pmc=8634575 |doi-access=free}}</ref> His book ''Fed Up'' (2026) tells the story of how humans evolved to be the planet's ultimate omnivores but never to choose their food, explores how and why there is no single optimal diet, argues against oversimple diets based primarily on elimination, and reviews the evidence that the healthiest diets are based primarily on unrefined plants.<ref name="fedup" />
